title: Distributed Systems & Cloud Computing
summary: A distributed system is a set of machines that fail independently and cannot agree on what time it is. This course builds the four mechanisms that make such a set behave like one service: causal clocks, a Raft consensus core, tunable quorum replication, and consistent hashing. Every algorithm is implemented against a deterministic message simulator, so a partition is something you cause on purpose and can replay exactly.
outcomes: Order events with Lamport and vector clocks, and justify when each is sufficient
Implement Raft leader election and log replication, including split votes and partition healing
Reason about the R + W > N quorum condition and show precisely where it fails to hold
Build a consistent-hashing ring with virtual nodes and measure key movement against modulo hashing
Apply hinted handoff, read repair and anti-entropy to reconcile replicas after a fault
Write deterministic fault-injection tests that reproduce a distributed failure exactly
State the CAP and PACELC trade-offs a given design has actually made
reading: Ongaro & Ousterhout, *In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)*, USENIX ATC 2014
DeCandia et al., *Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store*, SOSP 2007

modules.title: Time, causality and ordering
modules.summary: Ordering events without a shared clock: Lamport counters and vector clocks.
concepts: Physical clocks drift and skew; NTP bounds error but never removes it
The happens-before relation: program order, plus send precedes its receive, plus transitivity
Lamport clocks: a -> b implies L(a) < L(b), but the converse does not hold
Vector clocks: one counter per process; the ordering they induce is exactly happens-before
Two events are concurrent when neither vector dominates the other
Vector clocks cost O(processes) per message — the reason Dynamo prunes them
Total order by (Lamport, process id) is a tie-break, not a causal fact

read.title: Ordering without a clock: Lamport stamps and vector time
read.body:
Two data centres take the same customer's clicks. Frankfurt records an order at what its
clock calls 14:00:00.020. Nine milliseconds later the customer cancels it from a phone
that happens to be routed to Dublin, and Dublin stamps the cancellation 14:00:00.017 —
three milliseconds *before* the order it cancels. Both machines run NTP, both are inside
the ten milliseconds of error that NTP promises, and nothing is broken. A reconciliation
job that sorts by timestamp now sees a cancellation of an order that does not exist yet,
and depending on how it was written it either pages somebody at three in the morning or
quietly keeps the order and ships it.

The picture to hold is that a timestamp is a measurement with an error bar, and two
measurements whose error bars overlap do not order anything. Google's Spanner gets round
this by knowing the error bar and waiting it out before it commits; most systems cannot
afford the hardware that makes the bar small enough for that to be practical. So the
question this module asks is what can be said about order without consulting a physical
clock at all — and the answer turns out to be exactly what a correctness argument needs,
and no more.

## The order that is available without a clock

Strip the clocks away and three facts about order survive. A single process runs its own
events one after another, so an event it ran earlier comes before an event it ran later.
A message cannot be received before it is sent, so a send comes before its receive. And
if $x$ comes before $y$ and $y$ before $z$, then $x$ comes before $z$. Write $a \to b$,
read "$a$ happened before $b$", for the relation built from those three rules and nothing
else. It is a strong claim: $a \to b$ means there is a chain of program steps and messages
along which $a$ could have influenced $b$.

When neither $a \to b$ nor $b \to a$ holds, the two events are *concurrent*. That word
does not mean "at the same instant". It means no chain connects them in either direction,
so neither could have influenced the other, whatever the wall clocks said.

The lab in this module, *Lamport and vector clocks over an event log*, works on one log
of eight events across three processes, and it is worth tracing the arrows on it by hand
before writing any code:

```text
0  A local          A's first step
1  A send m1        0 -> 1 by program order
2  B local
3  B recv m1        1 -> 3 because m1 was sent before it arrived; 2 -> 3 by program order
4  B send m2        3 -> 4
5  C local
6  C recv m2        4 -> 6 and 5 -> 6
7  A local          1 -> 7 by program order
```

Follow the chains and event 0 reaches 1, 3, 4, 6 and 7. Event 2 reaches 3, 4 and 6 — but
never 7, because nothing B does ever arrives at A, and A's events 0, 1 and 7 form a chain
that receives nothing. So 2 and 7 are concurrent, and so are 5 and 7, and 1 and 5, and
nine more: twelve pairs in all.

## A counter that respects the arrows

Suppose you want one integer $L$ per event such that $a \to b$ guarantees $L(a) < L(b)$.
Take the three rules one at a time and see what each forces. Program order: every event
on a process needs a larger number than the previous one on that process, so keep a
counter per process and add one per event. Send before receive: the receive needs a
number larger than the send had, so put the sender's counter inside the message and, on
receipt, set the counter to $\max(\text{own}, \text{carried}) + 1$. The $\max$ is there
because the receiver may already be ahead of the sender; the $+1$ is the receive itself,
which is an event and needs its own number. Transitivity costs nothing, since $<$ is
transitive already. That is the whole of Lamport's clock, and every line of it was forced.

Trace it on the log. A's first two events are 1 and 2, and m1 carries 2. B's local step
is 1; the receive is $\max(1, 2) + 1 = 3$; the send is 4, and m2 carries 4. C's local
step is 1 and its receive is $\max(1, 4) + 1 = 5$. A's last step is 3.

```python
LOG = [
    ("A", "local", None),   # 0
    ("A", "send", "m1"),    # 1
    ("B", "local", None),   # 2
    ("B", "recv", "m1"),    # 3
    ("B", "send", "m2"),    # 4
    ("C", "local", None),   # 5
    ("C", "recv", "m2"),    # 6
    ("A", "local", None),   # 7
]

counter = {"A": 0, "B": 0, "C": 0}
carried = {}
stamps = []
for proc, op, arg in LOG:
    if op == "recv":
        counter[proc] = max(counter[proc], carried[arg]) + 1
    else:
        counter[proc] += 1
    if op == "send":
        carried[arg] = counter[proc]
    stamps.append(counter[proc])
print(stamps)
```

That prints `[1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 1, 5, 3]`, which is what the lab's `lamport_clocks` must
return. The order of the two operations on a receive matters: $\max$ first, then $+1$.
Adding one first and taking the maximum second gives B's receive $\max(2, 2) = 2$, the
same stamp as the send it received, and the rule the clock was built to keep is broken
on the very first message.

## The blind spot

Now look at events 2 and 7 again. They are concurrent, and they carry stamps 1 and 3.
The rule was built to make arrows produce increasing numbers; it never promised that
increasing numbers came from an arrow. A single number line has to put every event
somewhere, and two events with no relation between them still land at different places
on it. Read the stamps forwards and they are true; read them backwards — "1 is less than
3, so 2 happened before 7" — and they are fiction. The lab's `lamport_blind_spots` finds
every concurrent pair that a stamp comparison would nonetheless order, and on this log
there are two: $(2, 7)$ and $(5, 7)$.

## What one number threw away

Ask what information the counter discarded. When B received m1, its counter went from 1
to 3, which recorded "I now know of something numbered 2" — but not *whose* event that
was. Whether a chain exists from $a$ to $b$ is a question about which events of each
process $b$'s process had heard of at the moment of $b$. So keep a counter per process:
a vector, with entry $q$ holding how many of process $q$'s events have been heard of,
directly or through other processes.

The three rules now dictate three operations. An event on process $p$ adds one to entry
$p$. A send ships a copy of the whole vector. A receive takes, entry by entry, the larger
of its own value and the carried one — knowledge only grows, and the sender may know
more about some third process than the receiver does — and then adds one to its own
entry, because the receive is an event too. Merge first, then count: the merge brings in
everything the sender knew, and the increment records the one new thing that happened
here.

Comparison falls out of the meaning. $a \to b$ exactly when $b$'s process knew, at $b$,
of everything $a$'s process knew at $a$: every entry of $V(a)$ is at most the matching
entry of $V(b)$, and at least one is strictly smaller so that the events are not the same
one. If $a$ is ahead somewhere and $b$ is ahead somewhere else, no chain runs either way,
and the pair is concurrent.

Trace event 3: B holds $\{A:0, B:1, C:0\}$ and m1 carries $\{A:2, B:0, C:0\}$. The merge
gives $\{A:2, B:1, C:0\}$ and the increment $\{A:2, B:2, C:0\}$. Event 6: C holds
$\{A:0, B:0, C:1\}$, m2 carries $\{A:2, B:3, C:0\}$, the merge gives $\{A:2, B:3, C:1\}$
and the increment $\{A:2, B:3, C:2\}$. Event 7 is $\{A:3, B:0, C:0\}$, and A's vector
never learns anything about B or C, because A never receives. Compare 3 with 6:
$\{2, 2, 0\}$ against $\{2, 3, 2\}$ is at most everywhere and strictly less on B and C,
so 3 is before 6. Compare 2 with 7: $\{0, 1, 0\}$ against $\{3, 0, 0\}$ — 2 is ahead on
B, 7 is ahead on A, concurrent.

```python
LOG = [
    ("A", "local", None),   # 0
    ("A", "send", "m1"),    # 1
    ("B", "local", None),   # 2
    ("B", "recv", "m1"),    # 3
    ("B", "send", "m2"),    # 4
    ("C", "local", None),   # 5
    ("C", "recv", "m2"),    # 6
    ("A", "local", None),   # 7
]
procs = ["A", "B", "C"]
lamport = {p: 0 for p in procs}
clock = {p: {q: 0 for q in procs} for p in procs}
sent_stamp, sent_vec = {}, {}
stamps, vectors = [], []
for proc, op, arg in LOG:
    vec = clock[proc]
    if op == "recv":
        lamport[proc] = max(lamport[proc], sent_stamp[arg]) + 1
        for q, v in sent_vec[arg].items():
            vec[q] = max(vec[q], v)
    else:
        lamport[proc] += 1
    vec[proc] += 1
    if op == "send":
        sent_stamp[arg] = lamport[proc]
        sent_vec[arg] = dict(vec)
    stamps.append(lamport[proc])
    vectors.append(dict(vec))


def concurrent(a, b):
    return any(a[k] < b[k] for k in a) and any(a[k] > b[k] for k in a)


for i, v in enumerate(vectors):
    print(i, v)
pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(len(LOG)) for j in range(i + 1, len(LOG))
         if concurrent(vectors[i], vectors[j])]
print("concurrent pairs:", len(pairs))
print("ordered by Lamport anyway:", [(i, j) for (i, j) in pairs if stamps[i] < stamps[j]])
```

Eight vectors, twelve concurrent pairs, and the two that a Lamport stamp would have
ordered anyway: `[(2, 7), (5, 7)]`.

## The mistake people make

The first is reading Lamport backwards, and it is tempting for a good reason: on a single
process the counter *is* a total order, and in a busy system most pairs of events are in
fact connected by some chain, so the wrong reading is right most of the time and fails
only on the pairs that matter — the concurrent ones, which are precisely the pairs where
two replicas may have taken different actions.

The second is subtler and only shows up under delay. A send has to hand over a *copy* of
the vector. Hand over the live dictionary instead and every later local event on the
sender mutates a message that is still in flight:

```python
LOG = [("A", "send", "m1"), ("A", "local", None), ("B", "recv", "m1")]
for copy in (True, False):
    clock = {"A": {"A": 0, "B": 0}, "B": {"A": 0, "B": 0}}
    carried = {}
    for proc, op, arg in LOG:
        vec = clock[proc]
        if op == "recv":
            for q, v in carried[arg].items():
                vec[q] = max(vec[q], v)
        vec[proc] += 1
        if op == "send":
            carried[arg] = dict(vec) if copy else vec
    print("copy" if copy else "alias", "-> B after the receive:", clock["B"])
```

With the copy, B learns of one event on A, which is what had happened when m1 was sent.
With the alias, B's vector claims to know of A's second event as well — one that happened
after the send, and that no message ever described. B's receive now compares as *after*
an event it could not have seen. Nothing crashes, and the numbers look plausible, which
is the worst kind of bug a clock can have.

## Where it stops holding

The vector costs one entry per process on every message, whether or not that process has
ever done anything; the numeric unit in this module puts 200 processes at 4,800 bytes of
clock on a 120-byte payload. Dynamo keeps a vector per *object* rather than per cluster
and truncates it at ten entries, accepting that a pruned clock will sometimes report two
versions as concurrent when one did precede the other. The entries are also keyed by
process, so the set of processes has to be known and stable; a system where nodes come
and go has to decide what an entry means for a node that has left.

Both clocks see only the causality that their own messages carry. A user who reads a
balance on one screen and types it into a form on another has created a causal link that
no vector will ever record. And neither clock says a word about wall time: $a \to b$ says
$a$ could have influenced $b$; concurrent says it could not; nothing says which was
earlier on the calendar. When a replicated log needs every replica to apply operations
in one sequence, the pair (Lamport stamp, process id) gives a total order every replica
computes identically with no further messages — but it is a tie-break, chosen by
construction, and any reader who takes it for history is wrong about every concurrent
pair in it.

In the lab you will write both clocks over this log, `compare_vectors` with its four
outcomes, `concurrent_pairs` returning the twelve, and `lamport_blind_spots` returning
$(2, 7)$ and $(5, 7)$. Both clock functions must also refuse a receive with no matching
send and a message id sent twice — the guards are there because on a malformed log both
clocks keep producing numbers that look right.

quiz.title: What a clock can and cannot tell you

questions.q: You are handed two Lamport stamps and told $L(a) < L(b)$. What follows?
opts: $a$ happened before $b$
Nothing on its own — $a$ may have happened before $b$, or the two may be concurrent
$a$ and $b$ are concurrent
$a$ and $b$ ran on the same process
questions.why:
Lamport's rule runs one way only: if $a$ could have influenced $b$ then $L(a) < L(b)$.
Reading it backwards is the mistake, because a smaller stamp is produced both by a
genuine ancestor and by an event on some other machine nobody ever heard from. That is
what `lamport_blind_spots` in the lab is for — events 2 and 7 of the reference log are
concurrent and carry stamps 1 and 3, so a stamp comparison orders them anyway. Nor can
you read concurrency off the stamps: a causal chain also produces increasing numbers.
And two events on one process are indeed always ordered, but the stamps alone never say
they were on one process.

questions.q: Event $p$ carries the vector $\{A:2, B:1, C:0\}$ and event $q$ carries $\{A:1, B:3, C:0\}$. How are they related?
opts: $p$ happened before $q$
$q$ happened before $p$
$p$ and $q$ are concurrent
$p$ and $q$ are the same event seen twice
questions.why:
Dominance has to hold in every entry at once. $p$ is ahead on $A$ (2 against 1) and $q$
is ahead on $B$ (3 against 1), so neither vector dominates and neither event can have
influenced the other — they are concurrent. This is the whole gain over a Lamport stamp:
the vector detects the disagreement, and a single integer cannot, because collapsing
three counters into one number throws away exactly the information you need. Two
identical vectors would mean the same event; here nothing matches.

questions.q: Process $B$ holds $\{A:2, B:6\}$ and receives a message carrying $\{A:4, B:1\}$. What does it hold immediately after the receive?
questions.why:
Merge, then increment. Element-wise maximum first — $A$ becomes $\max(2,4) = 4$ and $B$
stays at $\max(6,1) = 6$, because the sender's view of $B$ is older than $B$'s own — and
then the receive is itself an event on $B$, so $B$'s own entry goes to 7. Stopping after
the merge loses the receive. Adding the entries instead of taking the maximum inflates
$A$ to 6 and claims knowledge of four events that never happened. Skipping the merge
leaves $A$ at 2, which is the bug that makes a message appear to arrive before it was
sent.

questions.q: Replicas order operations by the pair (Lamport stamp, process id). What has that bought them?
opts: A total order every replica agrees on, which says nothing about what caused what
A record of which operation caused which
The same ordering a vector clock would have produced
A guarantee that concurrent operations are never reordered
questions.why:
The tie-break is genuinely useful: it makes every replica apply the same operations in
the same sequence with no further communication, which is all a deterministic state
machine needs. What it is not is a fact about the world. It imposes an order on pairs
that had none, arbitrarily and by construction, so a consumer reading the sequence as
"this caused that" is wrong about every concurrent pair in it. A vector clock would have
left those pairs unordered, which is the honest answer and also a less convenient one.

questions.q: NTP holds every clock in the fleet within 10 ms of true time. A log line on machine X is stamped 4 ms earlier than one on machine Y. What may you conclude?
opts: X's event happened first
The two events are concurrent
Nothing about their order — the gap is smaller than the error the clocks admit to
Y's clock has drifted and needs resynchronising
questions.why:
NTP gives you a bound, not the truth. With each clock inside 10 ms of real time, stamps
4 ms apart are consistent with either event having happened first. An ordering claim is
only safe once the gap exceeds the sum of the two error bounds — which is precisely what
Spanner's TrueTime does when it waits out its uncertainty interval before committing.
Concurrency is not available either: that is a statement about causality, and a clock
reading knows nothing about who sent what to whom. Both clocks here are behaving exactly
as specified.

blanks.title: One event, stamped
blanks.brief:
The whole of vector time is four lines: absorb what the sender knew, then count the one
thing that is genuinely new. Get the order of those two wrong, or forget that a message
carries a *copy*, and the clock still produces plausible-looking numbers — which is the
worst failure mode available, because nothing crashes.

Nothing is executed here. You are choosing the operation, not writing the loop.
blanks.caption: the receive path, four holes

blanks.prompt: How does a receiver combine its own knowledge with the sender's?
opts: max
min
sum
abs
blanks.why: Element-wise maximum. Each entry is a count of events, and the receiver now knows about everything either side knew about, so the larger count is the true one.
whys: Element-wise maximum. Each entry is a count of events, and the receiver now knows about everything either side knew about, so the larger count is the true one.
Taking the smaller count throws away knowledge on receipt — the receiver would forget events it had already seen, and its vector would go backwards, which is the one thing a clock must never do.
Adding double-counts everything both sides already knew. Two processes that have exchanged a few messages would report counters far above the number of events that ever happened.
`abs` takes one argument and these counters are never negative, so it is not even applicable — worth noticing because the merge really is this simple, and there is nothing clever hiding in it.

blanks.prompt: By how much does the process advance its own entry for this event?
opts: len(clock)
v
blanks.why: By one, because exactly one event just happened here. Local work, a send and a receive all count the same — the receive is not special, it merely does the merge first.
whys: By one, because exactly one event just happened here. Local work, a send and a receive all count the same — the receive is not special, it merely does the merge first.

Not advancing at all means two distinct events on this process carry the same vector, so they compare as `equal` and the ordering the clock is supposed to induce quietly stops being a total order on one process's own timeline.

Jumping by the number of processes makes the counter grow with cluster size rather than with local activity, and comparisons against a process that has been quiet start returning `after` for no reason.
`v` is a counter that arrived from somewhere else. Using it here would let a chatty peer decide how fast this process's own time runs.

blanks.prompt: What does the message carry away?
opts: dict
list
sorted
iter
blanks.why: `dict(clock)` is a copy. Handing over the live vector means the next local event mutates a message already in flight, and the receiver merges a clock from the future — a bug that only shows up when the receive happens to be delivered late.
whys: `dict(clock)` is a copy. Handing over the live vector means the next local event mutates a message already in flight, and the receiver merges a clock from the future — a bug that only shows up when the receive happens to be delivered late.
`list(clock)` keeps the process names and drops every counter, so the receiver has no numbers to take a maximum against.
`sorted(clock)` has the same problem and adds an ordering nobody asked for: the keys come back as a plain list, and the counts are gone.
`iter(clock)` hands over a one-shot view of a structure that is about to change underneath it. Reading it after the sender moves on gives either stale keys or a runtime error.

blanks.prompt: What has to hold as well, for `a` to be strictly before `b`?
opts: any(a[q] < b[q] for q in a)
all(a[q] < b[q] for q in a)
any(a[q] > b[q] for q in a)
len(a) == len(b)
blanks.why: At least one entry must be strictly smaller, or `a` and `b` are the same vector and the events are equal rather than ordered. Dominance is `<=` everywhere plus `<` somewhere.
whys: At least one entry must be strictly smaller, or `a` and `b` are the same vector and the events are equal rather than ordered. Dominance is `<=` everywhere plus `<` somewhere.

Demanding every entry be strictly smaller is far too strong: a process that has been idle has the same count in both vectors, so an event genuinely in the past of another would be reported as concurrent.
Given that every entry already satisfies `<=`, no entry can be strictly greater — so this makes `before` permanently false, and every pair in the log comes back as concurrent.
Comparing lengths says the two vectors cover the same processes, which is true of every pair in a fixed cluster. It admits the equal case, so an event would be reported as strictly before itself.

numeric.title: How much clock rides on each message?
numeric.brief:
Vector clocks are the honest answer to ordering, and the bill arrives on every packet.
A vector is dense: one entry per process in the system, whether or not that process has
ever done anything, because a missing entry and a zero entry have to be told apart from
each other and from an entry you simply have not heard about yet.

This is the arithmetic that pushed Dynamo into truncating its clocks.
numeric.prompt: How many bytes of vector clock does each message carry?
numeric.note: Count the clock only, not the payload. A whole number of bytes.
numeric.figure: `[ payload 120 B ][ clock: (node id 16 B + counter 8 B) x one per process ]` — 200 processes, and every message carries the sender's entire vector.
numeric.aside: Dynamo caps the clock at ten entries and drops the oldest, accepting that two versions may then be reported as conflicting when one really did precede the other. Bounded bytes, occasional false conflicts.
numeric.hint: One entry per process, and each entry is a node id next to a counter. Nothing depends on how busy the processes have been.
numeric.wrong: The usual slip is to count only the processes that have a non-zero counter. The vector is dense — a process that has never been heard from still occupies an entry, because that is what distinguishes 'nothing yet' from 'not in the system'.
numeric.why: $200 \times (16 + 8) = 4800$ bytes, against a 120-byte payload: the bookkeeping is forty times the message. This is the cost that makes vector clocks unusable at fleet scale and perfectly reasonable at the scale of one key's replica set, which is why Dynamo keeps a clock per *object* — three or five entries — rather than per cluster. Halving the node id to 8 bytes only takes it to 3200; the term that hurts is the process count, and it is linear.

lab.title: Lamport and vector clocks over an event log
lab.brief:
An **event log** is a list of `(process, op, arg)` triples in the order an
external observer saw them. `op` is one of:

- `"local"` — internal work, `arg` is `None`
- `"send"` — `arg` is the message id being sent
- `"recv"` — `arg` is the message id being received

The reference log used throughout:

```python
LOG = [
    ("A", "local", None),   # 0
    ("A", "send", "m1"),    # 1
    ("B", "local", None),   # 2
    ("B", "recv", "m1"),    # 3
    ("B", "send", "m2"),    # 4
    ("C", "local", None),   # 5
    ("C", "recv", "m2"),    # 6
    ("A", "local", None),   # 7
]
```

## What to write

**`processes(log)`** — the process ids in first-appearance order. Raise
`ValueError` for an unknown `op`.

**`lamport_clocks(log)`** — one integer stamp per event, same order as the log.
Each process holds a counter starting at 0. A `local` or `send` event increments
it. A `recv` event sets the counter to `max(own, stamp carried by the message) + 1`.
A `send` records the stamp it carries. Expected for `LOG`:

```text
[1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 1, 5, 3]
```

**`vector_clocks(log)`** — one dict per event, mapping every process id to a
counter. A `recv` takes the element-wise maximum with the vector the message
carried, then increments its own entry. Event 3 above ends at
`{"A": 2, "B": 2, "C": 0}`.

**`compare_vectors(a, b)`** — one of `"before"`, `"after"`, `"equal"`,
`"concurrent"`. `a` is *before* `b` when every entry of `a` is less than or
equal to the matching entry of `b` and at least one is strictly smaller.

**`concurrent_pairs(log)`** — sorted `(i, j)` index pairs with `i < j` whose
vectors are concurrent. `LOG` has twelve of them.

**`lamport_blind_spots(log)`** — the subset of those pairs where
`lamport[i] < lamport[j]`. These are the pairs a Lamport stamp alone would
order, wrongly: `[(2, 7), (5, 7)]`.

Both clock functions must raise `ValueError` when a `recv` names a message that
was never sent, and when the same message id is sent twice.

hints: Keep one dict of counters keyed by process, and a second dict mapping message id to the stamp (or vector) that message carried.
For a receive, merge first and increment second — `max` over the carried value, then `+ 1` for the receive event itself.
Store a *copy* of the vector when a message is sent (`dict(vec)`), or later increments will mutate the message in flight.
`compare_vectors` needs both a strictly-less and a strictly-greater flag: both true means concurrent, neither true means equal.

modules.title: Consensus: Raft
modules.summary: Leader election and log replication on a deterministic message network.
concepts: State machine replication: identical logs applied in order give identical state
Terms as a logical clock — every message carries one, a larger term wins
Election safety: one vote per server per term, so at most one leader per term
The election restriction — a candidate needs a log at least as up to date as the voter's
Log matching: identical (index, term) implies identical prefixes
nextIndex backtracking is how a new leader repairs a divergent follower
A leader may only commit an entry from its *own* term; earlier entries commit indirectly
A split vote wastes a term; randomised timeouts, not cleverness, break the tie

read.title: One leader per term: how Raft keeps every log identical
read.body:
Three servers replicate a ledger. One of them, the primary, takes every write and copies
it to the other two. At 09:14 somebody unplugs the wrong cable in the rack, and for eight
seconds the two secondaries cannot reach the primary. They do the helpful thing and
promote one of themselves. The old primary, which can still see its clients, does not
know anything has happened and keeps accepting deposits. When the cable goes back in
there are two ledgers, each holding acknowledged writes the other does not have, and no
rule for choosing between them that does not lose money for somebody.

That is split brain, and Raft is a set of rules whose purpose is to make it impossible.
Two of them do most of the work: no two servers may believe they lead the same *term*,
and the server that ends up leading must already hold every write a client was told
about. Everything else in the protocol is bookkeeping in service of those two.

## Why a majority

A decision is made when a majority of servers agree to it. The reason is arithmetic. Two
majorities of five servers hold three each, and $3 + 3 = 6 > 5$, so they cannot be
disjoint — some server is in both. Enumerate every pair to see that there are no
exceptions:

```python
from itertools import combinations

servers = ["n1", "n2", "n3", "n4", "n5"]
majorities = [set(c) for c in combinations(servers, 3)]
disjoint = [(a, b) for a in majorities for b in majorities if not (a & b)]
print(len(majorities), "majorities of five, disjoint pairs:", len(disjoint))
print("smallest overlap:", min(len(a & b) for a in majorities for b in majorities))
```

Ten majorities, no disjoint pair, and the smallest overlap is one server. That one
shared server is the load-bearing member of every argument below. It voted once, so two
elections in a term cannot both have used it. It stored the committed entry, so a later
leader elected with its vote will be measured against a log that contains that entry. A
cluster of $2f + 1$ servers can therefore lose $f$ of them and still have a majority
left to decide things, and it can lose no more than that.

## Terms, and one vote each

Time is cut into terms, numbered from 1. Each term opens with an election and has at
most one leader, or none if the election failed. The term number is a Lamport clock in
the sense of the previous module: every message carries the sender's term, a server that
sees a larger term adopts it and becomes a follower at once, and a message carrying a
smaller term is rejected with the receiver's own term in the reply, so the stale sender
finds out and steps down. In the lab that check sits at the top of `handle`, before the
message type is even looked at, because it applies to all four kinds.

A server grants at most one vote per term, and it remembers who it voted for. Now two
candidates in the same term each need a majority, the majorities share a server, and
that server voted once — so at most one of them can win. This is the first of the two
guarantees, and it needed nothing but the counting above.

## One election and one entry, by hand

Three servers n1, n2, n3, all at term 0 with empty logs. An empty log has
`last_log_index() == -1` and `last_log_term() == 0`, and `commit_index` starts at $-1$.
The majority of three is two, and the leader counts itself.

```text
n1         start_election()      -> term 1, voted_for = n1, votes = {n1}
n1 -> n2   RequestVote           term=1  last_log_index=-1  last_log_term=0
n2 -> n1   RequestVoteReply      term=1  granted=True        (n2 adopts term 1)
n1         votes = {n1, n2}      -> 2 of 3: leader; next_index = 0 and match_index = -1 per peer

n1         client_append("set x 1")   -> index 0, entry (1, "set x 1")
n1 -> n2   AppendEntries         term=1  prev_log_index=-1  prev_log_term=0
                                 entries=[(1, "set x 1")]  leader_commit=-1
n2 -> n1   AppendEntriesReply    term=1  success=True  match_index=0
n1         match_index[n2] = 0   -> 1 + 1 = 2 hold index 0, own term: commit_index = 0
n2         commit_index = -1     -> nobody has told it yet

n1 -> n2   AppendEntries         term=1  prev_log_index=0  prev_log_term=1  entries=[]  leader_commit=0
n2         commit_index = min(0, 0) = 0
```

Read the lag at the end. The leader learns the entry is committed the moment the second
acknowledgement arrives; the follower learns it one full round later, from the
`leader_commit` field on the next `AppendEntries`, which was still $-1$ on the message
that carried the entry itself. The lab's replication test asserts exactly this: after one
round the leader's `commit_index` is 1 and n2's is $-1$.

## The election restriction

A leader repairs a follower by overwriting the follower's log with its own. That is what
makes the logs converge, and it is also what makes the second guarantee necessary: if a
server missing a committed entry could become leader, it would erase that entry from
every server it repaired. So a voter refuses any candidate whose log is behind its own.
The comparison is the last entry's *term* first, and only on a tie the last entry's
*index*:

```python
def at_least_as_up_to_date(cand_term, cand_index, my_term, my_index):
    return (cand_term > my_term or
            (cand_term == my_term and cand_index >= my_index))


# the voter holds [(1, "a"), (1, "b"), (3, "c")]: last term 3, last index 2
print(at_least_as_up_to_date(2, 5, 3, 2))
print(at_least_as_up_to_date(3, 2, 3, 2))
print(at_least_as_up_to_date(3, 1, 3, 2))
```

`False`, `True`, `False`. The first case is the one people get backwards. A six-entry
log whose last term is 2 loses to a three-entry log whose last term is 3, because a
term-3 leader existed, which means a majority voted for it, which means a majority's logs
were at least as good as that leader's — and the six-entry log never heard from term 3,
so its extra entries were never committed by anybody. Put the restriction next to the
majority argument and you get the second guarantee: a committed entry sits on a majority;
a candidate needs a majority; the server in both holds the entry and refuses a candidate
whose log is behind it; therefore every leader holds every committed entry.

## Log matching, and walking back

Every `AppendEntries` names the entry before the ones it carries, as `prev_log_index`
and `prev_log_term`, and the follower accepts only if it holds an entry with that index
and that term. By induction, two logs that agree on an (index, term) pair agree on
everything before it: the leader of that term created the entry once, in one position,
and never rewrote the prefix. A new leader that meets a rejection therefore lowers
`next_index` for that follower by one and tries again, until the check passes, and then
overwrites from there.

The lab's partition test produces exactly this. Server a led term 1 and was cut off with
b; it accepted three commands it could never commit, since two of five is not a majority.
Server c won term 2 on the other side and committed one entry. After the heal, c's log is
`[(1, w1), (1, w2), (2, z1)]` and a's is
`[(1, w1), (1, w2), (1, orphan0), (1, orphan1), (1, orphan2)]`:

```python
leader = [(1, "w1"), (1, "w2"), (2, "z1")]
follower = [(1, "w1"), (1, "w2"), (1, "orphan0"), (1, "orphan1"), (1, "orphan2")]
next_index = len(leader)
rounds = 0
while True:
    rounds += 1
    prev = next_index - 1
    prev_term = leader[prev][0] if prev >= 0 else 0
    entries = leader[next_index:]
    ok = prev < 0 or (prev < len(follower) and follower[prev][0] == prev_term)
    print("round %d: prev_log_index=%d prev_log_term=%d -> %s"
          % (rounds, prev, prev_term, "accepted" if ok else "rejected"))
    if not ok:
        next_index -= 1
        continue
    for offset, entry in enumerate(entries):
        i = prev + 1 + offset
        if i < len(follower) and follower[i][0] != entry[0]:
            del follower[i:]
        if i >= len(follower):
            follower.append(entry)
    break
print("follower now:", follower)
```

Round one asks a to confirm term 2 at index 2; a has term 1 there and refuses. Round two
asks about index 1, which matches, and the entry for index 2 conflicts on term, so
everything from index 2 is deleted and `z1` goes in its place. The three orphans are
gone, and no client was ever told they were committed, because a could count only itself
and b.

## The rule that looks wrong

There is one rule in Raft that reads like a mistake: a leader may not commit an entry
from an earlier term merely because a majority now stores it. It commits only entries of
its *own* term by counting, and earlier entries commit indirectly when a current-term
entry above them does.

Here is the case it guards against, with five servers. The leader of term 2 wrote an
entry at index 1, replicated it to one follower, and crashed. A server that never saw
index 1 won term 3 — three of the five were in the same state, so the election
restriction did not stop it — wrote its own index 1 with term 3 to itself alone, and
crashed too. The term-2 leader came back, won term 4 with the same three votes, and went
on replicating its old index 1, until three of five held the term-2 entry. If it now
declared index 1 committed, and then crashed, the term-3 server could win term 5 (its
last term, 3, beats their 2) and overwrite index 1 everywhere. An acknowledged entry
would vanish.

```python
def advance_commit(log, term, match_index, commit_index):
    majority = (len(match_index) + 1) // 2 + 1
    for n in range(len(log) - 1, commit_index, -1):
        if log[n][0] != term:
            continue
        count = 1 + sum(1 for m in match_index.values() if m >= n)
        if count >= majority:
            return n
    return commit_index


log = [(1, "w1"), (2, "w2")]
match = {"n2": 1, "n3": 1, "n4": -1, "n5": -1}
print("term-4 leader, three of five hold the term-2 entry:",
      advance_commit(log, 4, match, 0))
log.append((4, "w3"))
match = {"n2": 2, "n3": 2, "n4": -1, "n5": -1}
print("after a term-4 entry reaches the same three:",
      advance_commit(log, 4, match, 0))
```

The first call returns 0, the commit index it was given: three servers hold index 1, but
the entry's term is 2 and the leader's is 4, so it is skipped. The second call, once a
term-4 entry at index 2 has reached the same three servers, returns 2 — and index 1
commits with it, because a server holding index 2 with term 4 holds index 1 too, by log
matching, and no server whose last term is 3 can now win an election against a last term
of 4.

## The mistake people make

Forgetting that the leader counts itself. `advance_commit` needs `majority()` servers
*including* the leader, so it is `1 + sum(...)`; leave the `1 +` off and a three-server
cluster needs both followers for every commit, and one slow follower stalls the whole
service. It is tempting because "replicas" sounds like "the other machines", and because
a leader's own copy never arrives as a message. The second mistake is the client's:
reading a leader's *log* as if it were the committed state. The cut-off leader in the
partition test accepts three commands and replicates them to b, and its `commit_index`
never moves off 1. A client that reads the log sees writes that the cluster is about to
erase.

## Where it stops holding

Raft tolerates crashes and partitions, not lies: a server that sends a fabricated term
or a forged vote breaks every argument above, and a Byzantine setting needs a different
protocol and $3f + 1$ servers. It needs a majority alive; with five servers, three down
means no leader and no progress, which is the consistency side of CAP chosen
deliberately. It needs time to be roughly sane: elections are triggered by timeouts, and
randomised timeouts only break split votes if a message crosses the cluster much faster
than a timeout fires. And a leader that has not heard from a majority recently cannot
know it is still leader, so a read served from the leader alone can be stale unless it
first confirms its term with a heartbeat round.

The lab, *Raft election and log replication*, removes time from the picture on purpose.
Its `Cluster` moves nothing until `deliver()` is called, elections start when the test
calls `start_election()`, and the split vote is produced by dropping every `RequestVote`
but two rather than by racing timers — which is what makes that failure reproducible, and
what lets the partition test assert, message by message, that the minority side cannot
commit and that the heal converges every log to `[(1, w1), (1, w2), (2, z1)]`.

quiz.title: Terms, votes, and what a leader may commit

questions.q: A follower at term 5 receives an `AppendEntries` carrying term 4. What does it do?
opts: Adopts term 4 and appends the entries
Rejects it with `success=False` and stays at term 5
Starts an election at term 6
Appends the entries but refuses to advance its commit index
questions.why:
A message from a smaller term comes from a leader that has already been superseded and
does not know it yet. Rejecting it is the whole mechanism: the reply carries the
follower's own term, the stale leader sees a term larger than its own, and rule 1 makes
it step down. Adopting the smaller term would run history backwards. Appending the
entries — with or without committing them — would let a deposed leader keep writing to a
follower that has moved on, which is exactly the divergence the term is there to prevent.
Nothing here calls for an election: the follower has heard from a leader, just not a
current one.

questions.q: Why may a leader not commit an entry from an earlier term merely because a majority now stores it?
opts: Because such an entry can still be overwritten by a future leader, even with a majority holding it
Because entries from earlier terms are always duplicates of entries it already has
Because it cannot tell which term an entry came from
Because `match_index` from a follower in an earlier term cannot be trusted
questions.why:
This is Figure 8 of the Raft paper, and it is the least obvious rule in the protocol. A
majority holding an old-term entry is not enough, because a server whose log lacks that
entry can still win a later election — the election restriction compares the last entry,
not the whole log — and will then force its own log onto everyone. Committing it would
mean an applied entry disappearing. The fix is the rule in the lab's `advance_commit`:
only count an entry of your *own* term, and everything before it commits with it through
log matching. A leader can always read the term off an entry, since it is stored beside
the command, and `match_index` is reported by the follower's own current term.

questions.q: Four servers, and the vote splits two-two. What is the state of the cluster at the end of that term?
opts: The server with the lowest id takes office
Both candidates lead, each with its own half
No leader, nothing committed, nothing lost — a later term settles it
Deadlocked until an operator intervenes
questions.why:
A term that elects nobody is simply wasted: no entry can commit without a leader, and no
entry is damaged either. The retry is not cleverness, it is randomised timeouts — the two
candidates wake at different moments, one gets its requests out first, and the split does
not repeat. The lab reproduces this exactly, dropping all but two `RequestVote` messages
so both candidates stall on two votes out of four, then letting term 2 resolve it.
Lowest-id tie-breaking would make elections deterministic and is a real design, but it is
not Raft's, and two leaders in one term is precisely what one-vote-per-server-per-term
rules out.

questions.q: A voter refuses any candidate whose log is behind its own. What would break if it did not?
opts: Two leaders could hold the same term at once
A leader could take office missing committed entries and would then delete them everywhere else
The leader's log would grow without bound
Followers would never learn the commit index
questions.why:
Two guarantees are easy to confuse here. One vote per server per term is what stops two
leaders in a term, and it holds with or without the log comparison. The election
restriction does something else: it keeps a server that is missing committed entries out
of office. Without it, such a server could win, and since a leader repairs followers by
overwriting them, it would erase entries that had already been acknowledged to a client.
The comparison is `last_log_term` first, then `last_log_index` — the term dominates,
because a longer log from an older term is the log that is stale.

questions.q: A leader is cut off into a minority partition holding two of five servers. What can it still do?
opts: Nothing — it stops the moment the partition forms
Commit entries, since it is still the leader of the highest term it has seen
Elect a replacement leader on its own side of the partition
Accept client commands and replicate them, but never commit any of them
questions.why:
The leader has no way to detect the partition, so it keeps behaving normally: it appends
commands, sends `AppendEntries` to everyone, and gets replies from the one follower it
can still reach. What it cannot do is count to three. `advance_commit` needs a majority
including itself, and two is not a majority of five, so `commit_index` stops moving —
which is what the lab asserts after `isolate(["a", "b"])`. Meanwhile the other three
elect a leader at a higher term. When the link heals, the old leader sees that term,
steps down, and its uncommitted entries are overwritten. Availability was traded for
consistency, and this is the trade being made.

numeric.title: When does the leader know it is committed?
numeric.brief:
Commit latency in Raft is not the time to reach every replica; it is the time to reach
*enough* of them. The leader already holds the entry the instant it is appended, so it
needs the round trip to the followers that turn its own copy into a majority — and every
follower slower than those is irrelevant to the answer the client is waiting for.

That is the property worth internalising before tuning anything: a chronically slow
replica costs the cluster nothing at all while enough faster ones are healthy — and it
becomes the machine every commit waits on only once so few of those faster ones are left
that the majority cannot be reached without it.
numeric.prompt: How long after the command reaches the leader does the leader know the entry is committed?
numeric.note: Delays are one way; a reply takes the same time back. Processing and disk time are zero.
numeric.figure: `n1 (leader) —8ms— n2 · —11ms— n3 · —40ms— n4 · —95ms— n5` — five servers, one-way delays from the leader.
numeric.aside: The same cluster with n4 and n5 removed commits faster, not slower: a majority of three is two, the leader is one of them, so n2's reply at 16 ms is on its own enough. What the smaller cluster gives up is margin. Lose n2 and every commit falls onto n3 at 22 ms, and the tail latency of the cluster becomes the tail latency of that one machine.
numeric.hint: A majority of five is three, and the leader is one of them at zero cost. Which follower's reply is the one that tips the count over?
numeric.wrong: Two traps sit here. Forgetting that the leader counts itself pushes you to the third-fastest follower, and quoting a one-way delay forgets that the leader learns nothing until the acknowledgement comes back.
numeric.why: A majority of five is three. The leader has the entry at $t = 0$, so two follower acknowledgements are enough. `AppendEntries` reaches n2 at 8 ms and n3 at 11 ms; their replies land at 16 ms and 22 ms. At 22 ms the leader counts itself, n2 and n3 — a majority — and `advance_commit` moves. n4 and n5 contribute nothing to the answer, and would not even if they were down. The client's own latency is this plus the leader's reply to it; the *follower's* view of the commit arrives a further round later, on the next `AppendEntries`.

lab.title: Raft election and log replication
lab.brief:
`cluster.py` is given and read-only: a deterministic network with a FIFO queue,
cuttable links and a message dropper. Nothing moves unless you call
`deliver()`. You write `raft.py`.

## Message shapes

```text
RequestVote        term src dst last_log_index last_log_term
RequestVoteReply   term src dst granted
AppendEntries      term src dst prev_log_index prev_log_term entries leader_commit
AppendEntriesReply term src dst success match_index
```

A log entry is a `(term, command)` tuple. Indices are 0-based, so an empty log
has `last_log_index() == -1` and `last_log_term() == 0`. `commit_index` starts
at `-1`.

## `RaftNode(node_id, peers)`

Already initialised for you. Implement:

- `last_log_index()`, `last_log_term()`, `majority()` — majority is over the
  whole cluster, so `(len(peers) + 1) // 2 + 1`.
- `become_follower(term)` — state `"follower"`, adopt the term, clear
  `voted_for` and `votes`.
- `become_leader()` — state `"leader"`; every peer gets
  `next_index = last_log_index() + 1` and `match_index = -1`.
- `start_election()` — become a candidate, bump the term, vote for yourself,
  and return one `RequestVote` per peer. In a one-node cluster you are already
  the leader.
- `client_append(command)` — leader only; append `(self.term, command)` and
  return the new index. `ValueError` otherwise.
- `replicate()` — one `AppendEntries` per peer built from that peer's
  `next_index`. An empty `entries` list is a heartbeat. Non-leaders return `[]`.
- `handle(msg)` — dispatch. First: any message whose term exceeds yours makes
  you a follower at that term. An unknown `type` raises `ValueError`.

## The four handlers

**RequestVote** — grant when the terms match, you have not already voted for
someone else this term, and the candidate's log is at least as up to date
(higher `last_log_term`, or an equal term and an index that is not smaller).

**RequestVoteReply** — ignore unless you are still a candidate in that term and
the vote was granted. Add it; on reaching `majority()`, become leader and return
`replicate()`.

**AppendEntries** — reject with `success=False` when the term is stale, or when
`prev_log_index` is past the end of your log or holds a different term. Otherwise
step down to follower, overwrite from `prev_log_index + 1` where the terms differ,
append the rest, and set
`commit_index = min(leader_commit, prev_log_index + len(entries))` when the
leader is ahead. Reply with `match_index = prev_log_index + len(entries)`.

**AppendEntriesReply** — leaders only, current term only. On success record
`match_index` / `next_index` and try to advance the commit index; send more if
that peer is still behind. On failure decrement `next_index` (never below 0)
and resend.

The commit rule: the highest index `n` above the current `commit_index` such
that `log[n]` has *your* term and a majority of servers (you included) have
`match_index >= n`.

Note what the checks force you to notice — a follower learns an entry is
committed one round *after* the leader does.

class RaftNode:
    """One Raft server: follower, candidate or leader."""

    def __init__(self, node_id, peers):
        self.node_id = node_id
        self.peers = list(peers)
        self.state = "follower"
        self.term = 0
        self.voted_for = None
        self.log = []            # list of (term, command)
        self.commit_index = -1
        self.votes = set()
        self.next_index = {}     # peer -> next log index to send
        self.match_index = {}    # peer -> highest index known replicated

modules.title: Replication and tunable consistency
modules.summary: A quorum store with configurable N, R and W, plus read repair.
concepts: Leaderless replication: the client's coordinator writes to W and reads from R
R + W > N forces every read quorum to intersect every write quorum
Intersection gives read-your-writes only if the newest version wins the merge
W > N/2 is the separate condition that stops two concurrent writes both succeeding
Last-writer-wins by version discards data; the alternative is sibling values
Read repair is opportunistic anti-entropy carried on the read path
Availability versus staleness is a dial, not a binary — this is PACELC's ELC half

read.title: Quorums: what R + W > N buys, and what it does not
read.body:
A shopping cart lives on three replicas, a, b and c. A customer adds an item; the
coordinator that took the request writes to a and b, gets two acknowledgements, and
returns success — the write quorum was two, and c was slow, so nobody waited for it. A
second later the customer's page refreshes through a different coordinator, which reads
one replica because the read quorum is one, and the replica it happens to reach is c.
The cart comes back empty. No machine failed and no message was lost; the two operations
touched sets of replicas that did not overlap, and there is nothing in the arithmetic of
"two out of three" and "one out of three" that says they must.

## Reads and writes with no leader

In a leaderless store there is no primary to route through. Any node can coordinate a
request: it sends the write to the $N$ replicas of the key, waits for $W$
acknowledgements and returns; it sends a read to the replicas, waits for $R$ answers, and
returns the best of them. $N$, $R$ and $W$ are settings, and the lab in this module, *A
tunable quorum store*, is built so that you can set them and then aim a request at
particular replicas to see what the settings do and do not promise.

Here is the opening picture in twenty lines. The replicas are dictionaries, the
coordinator is two functions, and `order` is the sequence in which the coordinator tries
replicas — the lab calls it `contact_order` and lets a `prefer` argument put chosen
nodes at the front:

```python
replicas = {"a": {}, "b": {}, "c": {}}


def write(key, value, version, order, w):
    acks = []
    for node in order:
        replicas[node][key] = (version, value)
        acks.append(node)
        if len(acks) == w:
            break
    return acks


def read(key, order, r):
    answers = [(node, replicas[node].get(key)) for node in order[:r]]
    held = [got for _, got in answers if got is not None]
    return answers, (max(held) if held else None)


print("wrote to:", write("cart:7", "one item", 1, ["a", "b", "c"], w=2))
print("R=1 from c:", read("cart:7", ["c", "a", "b"], r=1))
print("R=2 from c:", read("cart:7", ["c", "a", "b"], r=2))
```

The write stopped after a and b. The read with $R = 1$ aimed at c saw `None`. The same
read with $R = 2$ picked up a as its second answer and returned `(1, "one item")` — and
notice that it returned the *versioned* value, because among `None` and
`(1, "one item")` the coordinator needs a rule for which to believe.

## Where the condition comes from

The read set has $R$ replicas and the write set has $W$, both drawn from the same $N$.
They can avoid each other only if there is room: $R + W \le N$. Demand $R + W > N$ and
they cannot fit side by side, so at least one replica is in both, and that replica holds
the write when the read arrives. The derivation unit in this module does the counting
symbolically; it can also be done by exhaustion, which makes the strictness of the
inequality hard to miss:

```python
from itertools import combinations


def disjoint_pairs(n, r, w):
    nodes = range(n)
    return sum(1 for rs in combinations(nodes, r) for ws in combinations(nodes, w)
               if not set(rs) & set(ws))


for n, r, w in [(3, 1, 2), (3, 2, 2), (5, 2, 3), (5, 3, 3), (5, 1, 5)]:
    print("N=%d R=%d W=%d  R+W>N: %-5s  disjoint read/write pairs: %d"
          % (n, r, w, r + w > n, disjoint_pairs(n, r, w)))
```

$N = 5$ with $R = 2$ and $W = 3$ is the row to stare at. Five is not greater than five,
and there are ten ways to pick a read pair and a write triple that share nothing.
Equality is not "nearly safe"; it is exactly the boundary at which disjoint sets become
possible. The lab's `read_your_writes(n, r, w)` is one comparison, and the tests hold it
to `(3, 1, 2)` being false and `(3, 2, 2)` being true.

## Versions, because overlap alone returns nothing

Intersection promises that one of the $R$ answers is fresh. It does not say which. So
every stored value carries a version, the coordinator hands out a fresh one for each
write from a counter that only goes up, a replica's `put` refuses anything whose version
is not strictly newer than what it holds, and a read returns the answer with the highest
version. Each of those three is load-bearing. Without the counter, two writes cannot be
told apart. Without the refusal, a slow write from the past could land on a replica after
a newer one and roll it backwards. Without the merge rule, the coordinator would return
whichever reply arrived first, which is the nearest replica and not the best informed
one.

The lab's tests probe the merge directly: write `old` to a and b, write `new` to b and
c, read from a and c, and the answer must be `new` — the highest version in the set, not
the first answer.

## What highest-version-wins throws away

The version counter is a total order, and the writes that produced it were not. Two
clients both read the cart at version 1, one adds eggs and one adds bread, and both write
back what they think the cart should now be:

```python
version = 0
replica = {}


def put(key, value):
    global version
    version += 1
    replica[key] = (version, value)
    return version


put("cart:7", ["milk"])
seen_by_x = replica["cart:7"]
seen_by_y = replica["cart:7"]
put("cart:7", seen_by_x[1] + ["eggs"])
put("cart:7", seen_by_y[1] + ["bread"])
print(replica["cart:7"])
```

`(3, ['milk', 'bread'])`. The eggs are gone, and nobody was told. This is last-writer-
wins, and it is a real design rather than a bug: it is cheap, every replica converges to
the same answer with no coordination, and for a sensor's latest temperature it is
exactly right. For a cart it is wrong, which is why Dynamo keeps both values as
*siblings* and hands the merge to the application — and why Amazon's cart is famous for
occasionally bringing back a deleted item, since a union merge never removes. Telling a
genuinely concurrent pair of writes apart from an ordered pair is the job of the vector
clocks from the first module; a counter cannot do it, because it collapses the two cases
into one number.

There is a second, separate condition hiding here. $R + W > N$ makes a read meet a
write. It says nothing about two *writes* meeting each other. With $W = 1$ on three
replicas, two writes can land on disjoint replicas and each replica holds one of them
believing it to be current; only $W > N/2$ forces the two write sets to share a replica,
so that at least one node saw both and can rank them. $N = 5$, $W = 3$, $R = 1$
satisfies the second condition and fails the first, so the two really are independent.

## Read repair

A read that assembled $R$ answers has, in its hands, evidence of which of those replicas
is behind. Throwing that away is wasteful, so the coordinator pushes the winner back to
every responder that returned an older version or nothing:

```python
replicas = {"a": {"k": (3, "new")}, "b": {"k": (3, "new")}, "c": {"k": (1, "old")}}
order = ["c", "a", "b"]
answers = [(node, replicas[node]["k"]) for node in order[:2]]
best = max(got for _, got in answers)
repaired = []
for node, got in answers:
    if got[0] < best[0]:
        replicas[node]["k"] = best
        repaired.append(node)
print("returned:", best, "repaired:", repaired)
print("c now holds:", replicas["c"]["k"])
```

This is anti-entropy done opportunistically on the read path, and it only ever touches
the replicas that actually answered — a replica that was down, or was not in the read
set, learns nothing from it. A background sweep over the whole preference list is a
different mechanism, and the capstone builds it as `repair(key)`.

## The mistake people make

The first is setting $R + W = N$ and calling it safe, usually because three plus two
"covers all five". The exhaustive count above shows ten ways it does not. The second is
subtler, and it comes from a lifetime of single-node databases: reading a failed write as
a write that did not happen.

```python
replicas = {"a": {}, "b": {}, "c": {}}
up = {"a": True, "b": False, "c": False}
acks = []
for node in ["a", "b", "c"]:
    if not up[node]:
        continue
    replicas[node]["k"] = (1, "v")
    acks.append(node)
print("acks:", acks, "-> quorum of 2 failed, but a holds:", replicas["a"])
```

The coordinator wanted two acknowledgements and got one, so it raises `QuorumError`.
Nothing takes the value back off a, because there is no undo log, no two-phase commit,
nothing anywhere that can roll a replica backwards. The next read that includes a will
see version 1 and repair everyone else to it. A failed write is a write with an *unknown*
outcome, and the lab's tests assert precisely this: after a `QuorumError`, the replica
that did acknowledge still holds the value. A client that needs "no" to mean "not stored"
has to be given a different store.

## Where it stops holding

Every argument above assumed both sets were drawn from the same $N$ home replicas. The
capstone deliberately breaks that with hinted handoff: when a home replica is down, a
node outside the preference list holds the write on its behalf and counts towards $W$.
That keeps writes available through a failure, and it means a read of the home replicas
can miss a write that was acknowledged, until the hint is delivered — a *sloppy* quorum
trades the intersection guarantee for uptime, and it is the right trade for a cart and
the wrong one for a bank balance.

The version counter lives on one coordinator. With many coordinators each running its
own counter, version 7 from one and version 7 from another are not comparable, and real
stores fall back on either wall-clock timestamps, which reintroduces every problem the
first module opened with, or on vector clocks. Nor does $R + W > N$ give
linearizability: a read that arrives while a write is halfway to its quorum can see the
new value on one replica, and a later read through a different set can see the old one,
because the write had not yet reached $W$ copies. What the condition buys is that a read
never misses a write that was *acknowledged* — and the same dials also set how many
nodes must be up for anything to work at all, since $W = N$ makes any single reboot a
write outage. Availability against staleness is a dial, and $R$ and $W$ are its two
knobs; that is the E-L-C half of PACELC, the trade a store makes even when nothing has
failed.

In the lab you will write `Replica.get` and `Replica.put`, the `QuorumStore` whose
`write` stops at $W$ acknowledgements and whose `read` stops at $R$, `contact_order` so
that a test can aim a read at c, `read_your_writes`, and the `repair=True` path that
records which responders were healed. The tests that matter most are the two that look
alike: the same write, read once with $R = 1$ and once with $R = 2$.

questions.q: With $N = 5$, which setting guarantees a read sees the last completed write while keeping reads as cheap as possible?
questions.why:
The guarantee needs $R + W > N$. That rules out $R = 2, W = 3$ immediately, since $5$ is
not greater than $5$ — the read set and the write set can be disjoint, which is the case
the lab reproduces on purpose. Of the three that qualify, $R = 1$ is the cheapest read,
and the bill arrives on the other side: $W = 5$ means every replica must be up for any
write to succeed. $R = 3, W = 3$ is the balanced choice most stores default to, and
$R = 5, W = 1$ is the mirror image — writes that survive almost anything, reads that
need the entire cluster. The condition does not pick a point on the line; it only says
which points are on it.

questions.q: $R + W > N$ holds and a write has returned successfully. What is a later read guaranteed to do?
opts: Contact at least one replica that acknowledged that write
Return that write's value, whatever the merge rule is
Contact every replica that acknowledged that write
Avoid contacting any replica that is behind
questions.why:
Intersection is all the arithmetic buys you: the two sets are too large to fit in $N$
replicas without sharing at least one. Turning that overlap into read-your-writes takes a
second ingredient — a version on every value and a merge that keeps the highest. Without
it the coordinator holds one fresh answer and some stale ones and no way to tell them
apart, which is the whole reason the store carries version numbers rather than bare
values. The read certainly does not reach every acknowledging replica; it stops the
moment it has $R$ responses. And it will often include a replica that is behind — read
repair exists precisely because it does.

questions.q: Why is $W > N/2$ a separate condition from $R + W > N$?
opts: It is a stronger form of the same condition and implies it
It forces two concurrent writes to share a replica, so one of them can be seen as older
It guarantees the read quorum is also a majority
It only matters when read repair is switched off
questions.why:
The two conditions constrain different pairs of quorums. $R + W > N$ makes a read set
meet a write set. $W > N/2$ makes two *write* sets meet each other, so at least one
replica sees both writes and can order them by version — without it, two clients can
write disjoint quorums, both succeed, and no replica anywhere has grounds to call either
one older. It is not the stronger condition: $N = 5, W = 3, R = 1$ satisfies $W > N/2$
and fails $R + W > N$, so a read can still miss. It says nothing about $R$, and read
repair changes when replicas converge, not whether two writes were ever comparable.

questions.q: The coordinator merges $R$ answers by keeping the highest version. What does that quietly discard?
opts: Nothing — the highest version is by definition the most recent write
The version numbers, which is why read repair has to run before the merge
A concurrent update that happened to draw a lower version
Every response that arrives after the first one
questions.why:
Versions are a total order; the writes that produced them were not. Two clients that both
read the old value and both write produce two values that are genuinely concurrent, and
last-writer-wins picks one and drops the other with no report to anyone. That is a real
choice, not a bug — it is cheap, it always converges, and for a "current temperature" it
is exactly right. For a shopping cart it is wrong, which is why Dynamo keeps both values
as siblings and hands the merge to the application, and why that cart is famous for
resurrecting a deleted item: union is a safe merge, and it never removes.

questions.q: A write with $W = 2$ raised a quorum error after one replica had already stored the value. What is now true?
opts: The value sits on that one replica, and anti-entropy will spread it
The value is discarded, because the write never reached its quorum
The value sits on that one replica and is rolled back by the next read
The coordinator retries the write at a lower $W$
questions.why:
There is no rollback anywhere in this design — no undo log, no two-phase commit, nothing
that could take a value back off a replica that has already stored it. A failed write is
not an absent write; it is a write with an unknown outcome, and read repair or anti-entropy
will happily finish the job the coordinator gave up on. The lab asserts exactly this after
a `QuorumError`, and the client is left in the genuinely awkward position of having been
told "no" about something that may yet become true. Retrying at a lower $W$ would be a
policy decision, and a store that made it silently would be lying about its own
guarantees.

blanks.title: Sizing the quorums for a keyspace
blanks.brief:
Every quorum store puts these dials in a config file and every one of them ships a
default that is wrong for somebody. Here the requirements are stated, so each dial has
exactly one defensible value — which is the point of the exercise: the settings are not
a matter of taste once you have written down what the service must survive.
blanks.caption: carts.yaml — four decisions, no code
blanks.listing:
# keyspace: carts
#
# Five replicas per key. The service must keep taking writes while a whole rack
# (two of the five nodes) is down, and a read must never miss a write that was
# acknowledged to the client.

replicas: 5
write_quorum: ___                 # W, as large as the rack outage still allows
read_quorum: ___                  # R, the smallest that pairs with that W
merge: ___                        # how the coordinator turns R answers into one
misses_an_acknowledged_write: ___ # the consequence of the three settings above

blanks.prompt: How large may W be if two of the five nodes are down?
blanks.why: With two nodes down only three can acknowledge, so W = 3 is the largest value a write can still satisfy during the outage. Every larger W turns a rack failure into a total write outage.
whys: W = 2 would work, but it gives up durability the outage did not force you to give up — and it drags R up to 4 to keep the pairing, making every read more expensive than it needs to be.
With two nodes down only three can acknowledge, so W = 3 is the largest value a write can still satisfy during the outage. Every larger W turns a rack failure into a total write outage.
W = 4 needs four live replicas. The moment the rack goes, every write raises a quorum error — the exact failure the requirement was written to avoid.
W = 5 demands the whole cluster for every write, so a single node reboot stops writes. This is the setting that makes availability numbers look inexplicable in a post-mortem.

blanks.prompt: Given that W, what is the smallest R that still meets the read requirement?
blanks.why: R + W > N with N = 5 and W = 3 needs R > 2, so R = 3. At R = 3 the read set and any write set share at least one replica, which is exactly the guarantee that was asked for.
whys: R = 1 gives R + W = 4, which is not greater than 5. A read aimed at the two replicas that were not in the write set misses the write entirely — the failure the lab reproduces deliberately.

R = 2 gives R + W = 5, and 5 is not greater than 5. This is the near miss worth remembering: the condition is strict, and equality is precisely the case where a read set and a write set can be disjoint.
R + W > N with N = 5 and W = 3 needs R > 2, so R = 3. At R = 3 the read set and any write set share at least one replica, which is exactly the guarantee that was asked for.
R = 5 satisfies the condition with room to spare and makes every read depend on every node, so a single failure stops reads — a much worse position than the writes were put in.

blanks.prompt: The coordinator has three answers in hand. Which one does it return?
opts: highest_version
first_response
majority_value
lowest_version
blanks.why: The overlap guarantees that one of the answers is at least as new as the last acknowledged write; taking the highest version is what turns that guarantee into the value the client gets back.
whys: The overlap guarantees that one of the answers is at least as new as the last acknowledged write; taking the highest version is what turns that guarantee into the value the client gets back.
Returning whichever reply arrives first hands the answer to the network. The fastest replica is usually the nearest one, not the best informed, and the intersection argument is wasted.
Counting votes among replicas is worse than it looks: after a W = 3 write to five replicas, a read of three can easily see two stale copies and one fresh one, and the majority is wrong.
Keeping the lowest version returns the stalest answer available, and read repair would then push that stale value back over the fresh one.

blanks.prompt: With those three settings, how often can a read miss a write the client was told had succeeded?
opts: never
sometimes
only while a node is down
only during a network partition
blanks.why: Never, and that is arithmetic rather than luck: three read replicas and three write replicas cannot both fit inside five without sharing one, and the merge keeps the newest of what comes back.
whys: Never, and that is arithmetic rather than luck: three read replicas and three write replicas cannot both fit inside five without sharing one, and the merge keeps the newest of what comes back.
'Sometimes' is the honest answer for R + W <= N, and the reason to state the requirement in the config rather than leave the dials to a default.
A node being down changes which replicas answer, not whether the sets overlap. It can stop the read from assembling R responses at all — that raises an error rather than returning a stale value.

A partition does not weaken the intersection either. It can leave a coordinator unable to reach R or W replicas, in which case the operation fails loudly; what it cannot do is let a successful read step over a successful write.

derive.title: Where R + W > N comes from
derive.brief:
A write is acknowledged by a set of $W$ replicas out of $N$. A later read collects
answers from a set of $R$ replicas out of the same $N$. Write $k$ for the number of
replicas that are in both sets.

Nothing below is about distributed systems. It is counting, and the famous condition
falls out of it in two lines.

steps.prompt: Write the number of distinct replicas touched by the two operations together — the size of the union — in terms of $R$, $W$ and $k$.
steps.hint: Inclusion–exclusion. Adding the two sizes counts each shared replica twice.
deconstruct: A replica in exactly one of the two sets is counted once by $R + W$.
A replica in both is counted twice, and there are $k$ of those, so subtract $k$.

steps.prompt: Both sets are drawn from the same cluster, so that union cannot exceed $N$. Rearrange $R + W - k \le N$ to get the smallest value $k$ can take.
steps.hint: Move $k$ to one side and $N$ to the other; the inequality flips to a lower bound on $k$.
deconstruct: $R + W - k \le N$ gives $R + W - N \le k$.
That is a floor, not an estimate: no choice of the two sets can do worse.

steps.prompt: The read is forced to touch the write when $k \ge 1$ for every possible pair of sets. What is the largest $N$ for which that still holds, in terms of $R$ and $W$?
steps.hint: Set the bound you just derived to at least 1 and solve for $N$.
deconstruct: $R + W - N \ge 1$ rearranges to $N \le R + W - 1$.
Which is the same statement as $R + W > N$, written the other way round.

steps.prompt: Now two *writes*, each acknowledged by $W$ replicas. By the same counting, what is the smallest number of replicas that must have seen both?
steps.hint: The bound was $R + W - N$ for any two sets of those sizes. Both sets now have size $W$.
deconstruct: Nothing in the counting cared that one set was a read and the other a write.

steps.prompt: Require that overlap to be at least 1 and solve for $W$: two write quorums always share a replica when $W$ exceeds what?
steps.hint: $2W - N \ge 1$ is $W \ge (N+1)/2$, and for a whole number of replicas that is the same as $W$ strictly greater than half of $N$.
deconstruct: Divide by two: $W \ge (N+1)/2$, which for integer $W$ is exactly $W > N/2$.

derive.closing:
Two different conditions have come out of one piece of counting, and they are about
different things. $R + W > N$ is a read *seeing* a write. $W > N/2$ is two writes seeing
*each other*. A store can satisfy one and fail the other: $N = 5$, $W = 3$, $R = 1$ has
write quorums that always overlap and a read that can still miss both of them entirely.

Notice also what the bound $k \ge R + W - N$ does not promise. It says at least one
replica in the read set holds the write; it says nothing about that replica being the one
whose answer you keep. The version numbers do that half, and a store with quorums and no
versions has bought itself nothing.

lab.title: A tunable quorum store
lab.brief:
`store.py` holds the logic; `main.py` is a demo. The checks import from
`store.py`.

## `Replica(node_id)`

A single storage node. `store` maps `key -> (version, value)`; `up` is a
boolean you flip to simulate a crash.

- `get(key)` — the stored `(version, value)` tuple, or `None`. Raises
  `ReplicaDown` when `up` is false.
- `put(key, version, value)` — store it only when it is newer than what is
  held. Returns `True` when the write was taken, `False` when it was rejected
  as stale. Raises `ReplicaDown` when down.

## `QuorumStore(replicas, r, w)`

`N` is `len(replicas)`. Raise `ValueError` for an empty replica list, duplicate
node ids, or an `r` or `w` outside `1..N`.

- `order` — the node ids in the order they were supplied.
- `contact_order(prefer)` — `prefer` first (in the order given), then every
  remaining node in `order`. `None` means just `order`. Raise `ValueError` if
  `prefer` names an unknown node.
- `next_version()` — a monotonically increasing integer, starting at 1.
- `write(key, value, prefer=None)` — take one fresh version, walk
  `contact_order`, skip nodes that raise `ReplicaDown`, and **stop as soon as W
  nodes have acknowledged**. Fewer than W acks raises `QuorumError` — after the
  writes that did land have already landed. Record the ack list in
  `last_write_set` and return the version.
- `read(key, prefer=None, repair=False)` — walk `contact_order`, skip down
  nodes, stop at R responses. Fewer than R raises `QuorumError`. Return the
  highest-versioned `(version, value)` seen, or `None` when every responder was
  empty. Record `last_read_set`. With `repair=True`, push the winner to every
  responder that was behind and record their ids in `last_repaired`.

## `read_your_writes(n, r, w)`

Return whether `r + w > n`. The point of the `prefer` argument is to let you
see this fail: with `N=3, W=2, R=1`, write to `["a", "b"]` and read from
`["c"]` and the read misses. With `R=2` no choice of read set can miss.

files.name: store.py
main.py
files.content:
from store import QuorumStore, Replica, read_your_writes

nodes = [Replica(name) for name in ("a", "b", "c")]
loose = QuorumStore(nodes, r=1, w=2)

version = loose.write("cart:7", "one item", prefer=["a", "b"])
print("wrote version", version, "to", loose.last_write_set)
print("R=1 reading from c:", loose.read("cart:7", prefer=["c"]))
print("read_your_writes(3, 1, 2):", read_your_writes(3, 1, 2))

strict = QuorumStore(nodes, r=2, w=2)
print("R=2 reading from c first:", strict.read("cart:7", prefer=["c"], repair=True))
print("repaired:", strict.last_repaired)

solution.name: store.py

hints: `put` rejects anything with `version <= current[0]`; a fresh key has no current version, so it always takes the first write.
`write` and `read` both stop the moment the quorum is satisfied — that early exit is exactly what makes a non-overlapping read possible.
A failed write is not undone. Collect the acks, then raise, and say so in the exception message.
Read repair happens after the winner is chosen, and only touches the replicas that were actually in the read set.

tests.name: Replica stores newest-wins and reports down
tests.code:
